rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Under Article 17(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, a provider of a high-risk AI system must put in place a quality management system ensuring compliance with the Regulation, documented systematically and orderly in written policies, procedures and instructions, and covering at least thirteen aspects. These are: (a) a strategy for regulatory compliance, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for managing modifications to the system; (b) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for design, design control and design verification; (c) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for development, quality control and quality assurance; (d) examination, test and validation procedures before, during and after development, and their frequency; (e) technical specifications, including standards, and where harmonised standards are not applied in full, the means used to meet the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements; (f) systems and procedures for data management, including acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation and retention; (g) the risk management system referred to in Article 9; (h) setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system under Article 72; (i) procedures for reporting serious incidents under Article 73; (j) handling of communication with national competent and other authorities, notified bodies, operators, customers and other interested parties; (k) systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information; (l) resource management, including security-of-supply measures; and (m) an accountability framework setting out management and staff responsibilities for all those aspects. Implementation must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation while preserving the requisite rigour and level of protection (Article 17(2)); providers already subject to sectoral Union quality-management obligations may integrate these aspects into that system (Article 17(3)), and financial institutions subject to Union financial services law on internal governance are deemed compliant except as regards points (g), (h) and (i) (Article 17(4)).
criteria_text: Regulatory compliance strategy incl. conformity assessment and modification management
Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the requirement for a regulatory compliance strategy including conformity assessment and modification management.
The answer includes design, development, quality control, and verification techniques and procedures under points (b) and (c).
The answer specifies examination, test, and validation procedures to be carried out before, during, and after development, and mentions their frequency.
The answer details data management procedures across the data lifecycle, listing multiple stages such as acquisition, collection, labelling, storage, and retention.
The answer explicitly references the Article 9 risk management system and the Article 72 post-market monitoring system.
The answer includes systems for record-keeping and an accountability framework outlining management and staff responsibilities.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with no self-reference or hedging; presents information in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h) unless and in so far as it is strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives. First, the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons (Article 5(1)(h)(i)). Second, the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack (Article 5(1)(h)(ii)). Third, the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of a criminal investigation or prosecution or executing a criminal penalty, for offences referred to in Annex II punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years (Article 5(1)(h)(iii)). Use is further conditioned on a completed fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registration of the system in the secure non-public section of the EU database, limited to the information listed in Article 49(4), points (a) to (d), namely Annex VIII Section A, points 1 to 10 except points 6, 8 and 9; Annex VIII Section B, points 1 to 5 and points 8 and 9; Annex VIII Section C, points 1 to 3; and Annex IX, points 1, 2, 3 and 5, accessible only to the Commission and the authorities referred to in Article 74(8).
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, and missing persons, matching the substance of criterion 1.
The answer includes the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety and a genuine terrorist threat, capturing the full substance of criterion 2.

The answer specifies the localisation or identification of a suspect for criminal offences listed in Annex II punishable by at least four years’ custodial sentence, which matches the requirement in criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: The response uses professional, neutral, and precise regulatory language, structured logically with clear reference to legal provisions, suitable for a compliance context.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Article 50(2) governs. Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the system's outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The technical solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, but only as far as technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of the various types of content, the costs of implementation, and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. The duty does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.
criteria_text: Marking must be machine-readable format
Marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated
Solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, as far as technically feasible
Feasibility judged against content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art
Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation
criterion_remarks: The answer states that outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format.
The answer explicitly says outputs must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
The answer includes that the solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible.
The answer references content-specific limitations, implementation costs, and the state of the art as factors for feasibility.
The answer lists all three exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input/semantics, and law enforcement authorisation.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information clearly without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, the obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models, and it entrusts the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office (Article 88(1)). Those exclusive powers are exercised taking into account the procedural guarantees under Article 94, and the delegation to the AI Office is without prejudice to the Commission's own powers of organisation and to the division of competences between the Member States and the Union under the Treaties (Article 88(1)). National market surveillance authorities therefore have no enforcement competence over Chapter V duties; they may only request the Commission to exercise the powers laid down in that Section where this is necessary and proportionate to assist with the fulfilment of their own tasks under the Regulation, without prejudice to Article 75(3) (Article 88(2)). Consistently with that allocation, providers of general-purpose AI models must cooperate as necessary with the Commission and the national competent authorities in the exercise of their competences and powers (Article 53(3)), and systemic-risk providers report serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities (Article 55(1)(c)).
criteria_text: European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V
AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer explicitly states that the Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V.
The candidate answer clearly states that the Commission entrusts the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Data collected and processed for the purpose of testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions may be transferred to third countries only provided that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented (Article 60(4)(e)). That is a cumulative condition: it operates alongside the other limbs of Article 60(4), so a lawful transfer presupposes an approved real-world testing plan, the required registration, establishment or a legal representative in the Union, and the informed consent of the testing subjects. The safeguards in question are those of Union data-protection law, including its international-transfer rules and the stricter conditions attaching to special categories of personal data. Because subjects may withdraw consent at any time and request immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data (Article 60(5)), the transfer arrangement must remain capable of giving effect to that deletion. The supplied evidence contains no text supporting any Article 10(5) limb.
criteria_text: Appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the substance of the criterion by explicitly requiring appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law for the transfer of data to third countries.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow, suitable for a regulatory compliance context.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the conditions are alternatives, not cumulative. Article 51(1) provides that a general-purpose AI model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk "if it meets any of the following conditions", so satisfying one suffices. The first condition, Article 51(1)(a), is that the model has high-impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; "high-impact capabilities" means capabilities that match or exceed those recorded in the most advanced general-purpose AI models (Article 3(64)). The second, Article 51(1)(b), is a decision of the Commission, taken ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, that the model has capabilities or an impact equivalent to point (a), having regard to the criteria in Annex XIII. Article 51(2) adds a presumption, not a third condition: a model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities under point (a) where the cumulative computation used for its training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10²⁵. Article 51(3) empowers the Commission to amend those thresholds by delegated acts.
criteria_text: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of the presumption based on training compute exceeding 10^25 FLOPs, citing Article 51(2) and specifying the threshold.

The answer clearly explains that a Commission decision, either ex officio or following a qualified alert, based on equivalence to point (a) and considering Annex XIII criteria, constitutes the second condition.
The answer explicitly states that the conditions are alternatives, not cumulative, and correctly quotes the phrase 'if it meets any of the following conditions' to support this.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with logical structure and complete sentences, suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No. An AI safety component of an MDR Class I device of that kind is not automatically high-risk, because Article 6(1) requires both of its conditions to be fulfilled. Article 6(1)(a) is met: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices is Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, point 11. Article 6(1)(b) is not met: such a Class I device, non-sterile, without a measuring function, and not a reusable surgical instrument, is self-certified by the manufacturer and is not required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment. It would still be high-risk under Article 6(2) if it falls within an Annex III use-case.
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the position, which matches the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that both conditions of Article 6(1) must be fulfilled, conveying the cumulative nature of the conditions.
The answer correctly explains that the specified MDR Class I device is self-certified and does not require third-party conformity assessment.
The answer concludes that because condition (b) is not met, Article 6(1) does not apply, which directly satisfies the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents reasoning logically for a regulatory context.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a lift qualifies as high-risk under Article 6(1), provided both cumulative conditions are fulfilled. First, under Article 6(1)(a), it must be intended to be used as a safety component of a product, the lift, covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which at Annex I, point 4 lists Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts and safety components for lifts. Second, under Article 6(1)(b), the lift whose safety component the AI system is must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that Directive. The Article 6(1) chapeau makes this classification apply irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift. Because this is the Annex I product route, the Article 6(3) derogation, which is confined to Annex III systems, is unavailable. Under Article 43(3) the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required by Directive 2014/33/EU, with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment.
criteria_text: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word and maintains that position throughout.
The answer states the AI system must be intended as a safety component of a lift, which is covered by Directive 2014/33/EU listed in Annex I.
The answer specifies that the lift must be required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the applicable Directive.
The answer explicitly refers to 'both cumulative conditions' and structures the explanation around their joint fulfillment.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with logical structure and precise references; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
rows.answer: ‘risk’ means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm;
criteria_text: Combination of probability of occurrence of harm and severity of that harm
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the full substance of the definition of 'risk' as set out in Article 3.2, using the exact wording from the regulation.
rows.tone_remark: The response is concise, professional, and uses the precise regulatory language without any self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Both duties apply, and both are immediate; the market surveillance authority's role does not displace either. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions, to bring it into conformity, withdraw, disable or recall it, as appropriate, and inform the distributors and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and importers. Under Article 20(2), where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it must immediately investigate the causes, in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body that issued the certificate under Article 44, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken. The authority's evaluation under Article 79(2) runs in parallel; the operator must still ensure appropriate corrective action for all systems concerned made available on the Union market (Article 79(4)), failing which provisional measures follow under Article 79(5).
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that both duties apply and are immediate.
The answer cites Article 20(1) and describes the provider's duty to take immediate corrective action when non-compliance is suspected.
The answer states that under Article 20(2), the provider must immediately investigate the causes, establishing it as a direct obligation.
The answer clarifies that investigation is done in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and emphasizes that the provider has an active duty, not deferred to the authority.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with precise references; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model did not hallucinate: Article 24(3) imposes exactly that duty. Distributors must ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise the system's compliance with the requirements set out in Section 2. The qualifier "where applicable" answers the operator's objection, it bites where the system is embedded in or supplied with a physical product or medium, and where the CE marking, the copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the instructions for use the operator must verify under Article 24(1) travel with it and can be lost, damaged or altered. If you then have reason to consider a system you made available non-conforming, Article 24(4) requires corrective action, withdrawal or recall, and, where it presents an Article 79(1) risk, immediate information to the provider or importer and the competent authorities.
criteria_text: No, not hallucinated
Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly confirms that the model did not hallucinate, affirming the correctness of the operator's information.
The answer directly states that Article 24(3) imposes the duty in question, citing the provision and its substance.

The answer explains that the duty applies 'where applicable', clarifying that it pertains when the system is embedded in or supplied with physical media or products, and elaborates on the relevance of physical handling to compliance documentation.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow, suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: Nothing in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 prohibits or classifies drones as such; the use decides. Under Article 6(1) a drone's AI is high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment; under Article 6(2), AI listed in Annex III is high-risk irrespective of the platform. Using a drone to identify who is around town is biometric identification: Annex III.1(a) makes remote biometric identification systems high-risk, and Article 5(1)(h) prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement unless strictly necessary for targeted search for abduction/trafficking/sexual-exploitation victims or missing persons (i), prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or of a terrorist attack (ii), or localisation of a suspect of an Annex II offence punishable by at least four years (iii). A toy drone changes only the Article 6(1) route: toys fall under Annex I.2 (Directive 2009/48/EC), so its AI is high-risk only where that Directive requires third-party assessment, the toy label itself grants no exemption, and the same surveillance use would still engage Annex III.1(a). For toy drones in other applications, classification again follows Article 6(1) and the Annex III intended purpose, with Article 50(1) requiring disclosure where the system interacts directly with natural persons.
criteria_text: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)
criterion_remarks: States that classification depends on intended use under Article 6, not the drone itself.
Correctly identifies use in public to identify people as remote biometric identification, falling under Annex III(1)(a) and not the verification exclusion.
Explains that toy status does not exempt from high-risk classification and that the determination depends on intended use and applicable conformity assessment.
Clarifies that for other applications, risk classification still depends on Article 6(1) or Annex III criteria, consistent with the intended use.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear regulatory prose without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, you cannot simply proceed, and yes, the operator must keep the logs. Article 26(1) requires deployers to use a high-risk AI system in accordance with the instructions for use, which under Article 13(3)(b)(i) state its intended purpose; a use outside that purpose is not a compliant deployer use. Under Article 25(1), a deployer that modifies the intended purpose of a high-risk AI system is considered a provider of it and assumes the full provider obligations, including conformity assessment, with the initial provider owing cooperation under Article 25(2). The operator's legal team's "no risk" view does not de-classify the system: the Annex I route (Article 6(1)) turns on whether the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I points 1 to 20 and subject to third-party conformity assessment, while the Annex III route (Article 6(2)) turns on listed use cases; the Article 6(3) derogation is a documented provider self-assessment, not a deployer judgement, and never applies where the system profiles natural persons. On logging, Article 26(6) obliges the operator to retain the automatically generated logs under the operator's control for at least six months. The evidence supplies no text for Articles 10(2), 12(2) or 43(1), so those limbs are not addressed.
criteria_text: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you cannot simply proceed,' which matches the required verdict.

The answer explains that Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use, and that deviating from intended use is non-compliant, referencing Article 13(3)(b)(i) and the concept of intended purpose.
The answer affirms that logging is required under Article 26(6) for at least six months, regardless of the specific use, and notes the condition of log control.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents actionable regulatory analysis.

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes, AI software that supports clinicians' treatment decisions is potentially high-risk, under Article 6(1) read with Annex I, section 11 (Regulation (EU) 2017/745, MDR) or section 12 (Regulation (EU) 2017/746, IVDR). Article 6(1) requires cumulatively that (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation, and (b) that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that same legislation. Treatment-recommendation software that is a medical device above Class I satisfies both limbs. The Article 6(3) derogations (narrow procedural task, preparatory task, and the profiling override) are unavailable here: they bite only on the Annex III route, not on the Annex I product route.
criteria_text: Yes
Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the AI software is potentially high-risk, which affirms the 'Yes' criterion.
The answer cites Article 6(1), not Article 6(2), and explains the high-risk classification via the Annex I product route, not the Annex III route specified in the criterion.
The answer does not mention Annex III or link the AI system to healthcare access/provision under Annex III; instead, it bases the high-risk classification on Annex I and medical device regulations.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; uses precise regulatory language without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Yes, yes, yes, yes, no, under Article 53(1)(b), the information supplied to downstream providers must contain at least the Annex XII elements. Annex XII.1 expressly requires the date of release and methods of distribution (point (c)); how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself, where applicable (point (d)); the architecture and number of parameters (point (f)); and the licence for the model (point (h)). Samples of outlier training data are not required: Annex XII.2(c) asks only for information on the data used for training, testing and validation, including type, provenance and curation methodologies, not data samples or outlier examples.
criteria_text: Date of release - Yes
Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the date of release must be disclosed, aligning with the requirement in Annex XII.1(c).
The answer clearly confirms disclosure of architecture and number of parameters, referencing Annex XII.1(f).
The answer affirms disclosure of interaction with hardware or software, citing Annex XII.1(d).
The answer confirms license disclosure, pointing to Annex XII.1(h).
The answer correctly states that samples of outlier training data are not required, explaining that only information about data type, provenance, and curation is required under Annex XII.2(c).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with precise references; no self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, "healthcare decision-making" is not itself one of the listed areas, though several healthcare-related uses are high-risk. The eight areas of Annex III are: biometrics (Annex III.1); critical infrastructure (Annex III.2); education and vocational training (Annex III.3); employment, workers management and access to self-employment (Annex III.4); access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits (Annex III.5); law enforcement (Annex III.6); migration, asylum and border control management (Annex III.7); and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III.8). Under Article 6(2), only a lettered use-case within an area makes a system high-risk. Healthcare enters through Annex III.5: point (a) covers systems used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them; point (c) covers risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance; point (d) covers emergency call evaluation and dispatch, including emergency healthcare patient triage. Separately, under Article 6(1), AI that is a medical or in vitro diagnostic device, or a safety component of one, under Annex I.11 to 12 requiring third-party conformity assessment is high-risk.
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No
criterion_remarks: The answer lists all eight areas of high-risk use cases as specified in Annex III, using equivalent wording and clear references.
The answer explicitly states that 'healthcare decision-making' is not itself one of the listed areas, which matches the required 'No' verdict.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Adding guardrails cannot move a system out of high-risk, and Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted recognises no "moderate risk" tier for AI systems. Classification is fixed by Article 6: either the Annex I product route (safety component of, or a product under, Annex I harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment) or an Annex III listed use-case. Guardrails are risk-control measures under Article 9 and Article 8(1); they are documented, not declassifying, recorded in the Annex IV technical documentation as the general description, design specifications, architecture and computational resources, and risk-management measures, logged under Article 12(2)(a)-(c) (start/stop, input reference data, events for post-market monitoring), and disclosed in the instructions for use under Article 13(3)(b)(i)-(vii): intended purpose; accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels; foreseeable circumstances including reasonably foreseeable misuse creating Article 9(2) risks; explanatory technical capabilities; performance for specific persons or groups; input-data and training/validation/testing specifications; and information enabling deployers to interpret outputs. Changing capabilities and intended purpose can change classification, since Article 6(2) keys to the Annex III use-case and Article 6(3) exempts systems posing no significant risk that perform only a narrow procedural task, improve a completed human activity, detect decision patterns without replacing human assessment, or perform a preparatory task, never where the system profiles natural persons, with the self-assessment documented before placing on the market. Conversely, modifying intended purpose so a system becomes high-risk makes the modifier a provider under Article 25(1)(c).
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states that guardrails alone do not create a 'moderate risk' tier and that the Act only allows a binary classification under Article 6(3), thus conveying the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly lists the four conditions in Article 6(3) under which an Annex III system may be exempted from high-risk classification, directly stating the substance of criterion 2.

The answer confirms that changing the system's capabilities and intended purpose can change its classification if the new purpose meets one of the Article 6(3) conditions, satisfying the substance of criterion 3.

The answer explicitly states that a system performing profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or changes to intended use, which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: The response uses professional, neutral, third-person language, avoids self-reference or hedging, and presents information in a structured, coherent manner suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, such use is permitted: generating synthetic clinical images for teaching is not among the practices prohibited by Article 5(1), and university illustration does not itself make the system high-risk. However, the artificial nature must be disclosed. Images that resemble real persons or conditions and would falsely appear authentic are deep fakes within Article 3(60), so the university, as deployer, must disclose under Article 50(4) that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The lighter regime is not available: the law-enforcement exemption in Article 50(4) covers only use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, and the reduced "appropriate manner" disclosure applies only to evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works, not to educational material. The provider must separately mark outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format under Article 50(2).
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that generating synthetic clinical images for teaching is not prohibited, hence permitted.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4) for deep fakes, including those used in university settings.
The answer states the lighter regime does not apply to educational material, directly contradicting the criterion that it does apply as an analogous work.
The answer correctly distinguishes the law-enforcement carve-out as inapplicable and notes it is a full exemption, not a lighter regime.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No, this is not high-risk on the facts given, and it is not prohibited either. High-risk status under Annex III requires a listed use-case: the law-enforcement area (Annex III, point 6) covers use by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, which a retailer's own loss-prevention tool is not, and no other listed area (biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, migration, justice) is engaged. Article 5(1)(d) is likewise not met: it bars assessing or predicting the risk of a person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or personality traits, and expressly does not apply to systems supporting human assessment already based on objective and verifiable facts linked to the activity, here, current-cart and checkout anomalies, with staff deciding. Article 5(1)(c) fails too: no evaluation over a certain period producing a social score causing cross-context (i) or disproportionate (ii) detriment.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, this is not high-risk on the facts given', which matches the required verdict.
The answer states that Annex III.6 applies only to use by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities and explicitly notes the retailer's tool does not meet that condition.
The answer explains that a retailer's loss-prevention tool run by store staff is not used by or on behalf of law enforcement, hence falling outside Annex III.6, regardless of functional resemblance.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents reasoning coherently for a compliance context.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, you cannot skip Chapter III, Section 2. Article 43(3) provides that for high-risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, the requirements set out in Section 2 apply to those systems and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment. Its final subparagraph governs the operator's exact facts: where a Section A act enables the product manufacturer to opt out of third-party conformity assessment on condition that it has applied all harmonised standards covering the relevant requirements, that manufacturer may use that option only if it has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41 covering all requirements set out in Section 2. The opt-out therefore changes the route of demonstrating conformity, not the substance of the obligations, and using it without standards coverage of Section 2 makes the opt-out itself unavailable. Annex I items 1 to 12 are the Section A acts to which that subparagraph attaches; items 13 to 20 are Section B. Article 43(1), points (a) to (d), concerns Annex III point 1 systems and is not the operator's route. The evidence supplied contains no text for Article 41(1), point (a)(i), (iv).
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you cannot skip Chapter III, Section 2', which matches the required 'No' verdict.
The answer explicitly states that Section 2 requirements apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment, citing the second sentence of Article 43(3).

The answer explains that the opt-out is available only if harmonised standards or common specifications cover all Section 2 requirements, directly reflecting the condition in the final subparagraph of Article 43(3).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents legal analysis in a way usable by a compliance professional.
